# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 87 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 87 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_087_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 9, Chapter 4

**1** When the tower was finished, the tall man called me and said, "Come, let us go and eat with the virgins." We sat down together at a table, and the tall man placed twelve urns full of wine on the table, and bread was also there, and he ate and drank with us. **2** After we had eaten and drunk, the tall man called the virgins and said to them, "Guard this man and do not let him go away tonight." The virgins said to me, "You will sleep here with us tonight as a brother, not as a husband — for you are our brother, and from this day we will dwell with you, for we love you greatly." **3** I was ashamed to remain with them. But the one who seemed to be the chief among them began to embrace me, and the others, seeing this, also embraced me; and they led me around the tower and played with me. **4** And I became as it were youthful again, and began to play with them; for some danced and others sang, and I walked with them around the tower in silence, rejoicing with them. **5** When evening came I wished to go into the house, but they would not let me go. We remained through the night, and I slept in the tower. **6** The virgins spread out their fine linen garments on the ground and made me lie down in the middle of them, and they did nothing whatever except pray; and I also prayed with them without ceasing, and the virgins rejoiced greatly. I remained with the virgins until morning, when the shepherd came.

---

### Translator's Note
This remarkable scene — Hermas feasting, playing, and keeping vigil with the twelve virgins who are the powers of the Son of God — is one of the most unusual passages in early Christian literature. The renewal of youth (v. 4) signals the transformative effect of virtue on the soul. The all-night prayer vigil (v. 6) mirrors early church practice. SOPHIA follows LOGOS; PNEUMA's "overjoyed" and "deeply" add emotional intensification not in the Greek.
